messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Doctor
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 54

# The Weight of the White Coat

Roberto is a 67-year-old Colombian-born internist who has practiced medicine in the United States for nearly four decades. He is soft-spoken, precise in his language, and carries himself with the composed authority that comes from a lifetime of being the person in the room who is supposed to have answers. He has never married, though he came close once. He lives alone in a modest apartment near the hospital where he still works three days a week, surrounded by medical journals he no longer reads with the same appetite he once did.

Eighteen years ago, Roberto's eleven-year-old son, Diego — who lived primarily with his mother in Bogotá following their separation — was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Roberto learned of it over the phone, a Tuesday morning between patients. He remembers the fluorescent hum of the hallway, the weight of the receiver, the way his own medical knowledge became a kind of weapon turned against him. He understood, with clinical precision, exactly how bad it could get.

He flew to Colombia within forty-eight hours and spent the next fourteen months navigating a terrifying middle space — neither Diego's primary caregiver nor a detached observer, but a physician-father who knew too much and could control almost nothing. He sat beside Diego's hospital bed watching infusions drip and interpreting every lab value with an expertise that brought him no comfort. There were two episodes of septic crisis during which Roberto genuinely believed he was watching his son die. Diego survived. He is now a healthy twenty-nine-year-old living in Medellín, married, with a daughter of his own.

Roberto will tell you, quietly, that Diego is fine. What Roberto does not say easily is that he is not.

The intrusions began while Diego was still in treatment and never fully stopped. Roberto wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart already racing, pulled from sleep by images he cannot always name upon waking — the blue tint of Diego's lips during one crisis, the particular sound of a cardiac monitor's alarm, the face of the oncologist delivering a complication update. He lies in the dark and runs through the memory like a film he cannot switch off, his body convinced the emergency is still happening.

At the hospital, Roberto is competent and respected. But pediatric cases have become nearly impossible for him. When he encounters a seriously ill child — or even hears colleagues discussing one — he feels a physical constriction in his chest, a narrowing of his vision, a desperate urge to leave the floor. He has quietly arranged his practice to minimize such encounters, a fact he has never disclosed to his department chief. He tells himself this is a matter of specialization.

He has become, over the years, someone who keeps people at a careful distance. Colleagues describe him as reserved. He declines most social invitations, finding that gatherings feel effortful in a way they did not before — as though he is performing a version of himself that no longer quite fits. He drinks two glasses of scotch most evenings, which he monitors carefully, telling himself that monitoring it means it is not a problem.

What troubles Roberto most, when he allows himself to examine it, is the guilt that has never loosened its grip. He was a physician. He understood the disease. And still he felt helpless — worse than helpless, useless — sitting in that hospital room in Bogotá. He has never been able to reconcile the doctor he believes himself to be with the father who sat in a plastic chair and wept in a bathroom stall so his son would not hear him. He carries this as a private failure, tucked beneath the white coat he still puts on three mornings a week, walking into a hospital where everyone assumes he is fine because he has always appeared to be.
